title: AI in Education #4: Five Things I Learned from Carl Hendrick
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton distills five takeaways from a conversation with Carl Hendrick, a 20-year classroom veteran turned cognitive-science researcher now working with Alpha School, who argues -- against fellow guest Adam Boxer -- that AI-driven ed-tech really is different this time because it is grounded in the science of learning rather than digitised worksheets. Hendrick's most pointed claim is that retrieval practice has become 'the most lethally mutated thing in education': schools tick the box with shallow cramming while ignoring spacing and forgetting curves. That claim tracks a real research finding Barton folds in from Tom Perry's EEF-commissioned review of cognitive science in the classroom, which found that while lab studies of retrieval practice show consistently positive, replicable effects, studies run in actual school settings show much smaller and more variable effects -- exactly the gap between sound principle and diluted classroom practice that Hendrick is describing. He offers an inside look at Alpha School that complicates the caricature: chatbots and phones are banned, staff ('guides') give one-to-one attention driven by system data, but the model costs upwards of $40,000 a year and its outcome data remains private. He argues AI could also capture the sequencing judgment of the best curriculum designers for teachers who never develop it themselves, and predicts that AI-scale data on millions of students will finally give the science of learning the resolution it has always lacked. Barton concludes the piece is genuinely a coin flip between Boxer's scepticism and Hendrick's optimism.
points: Hendrick's argument for 'this time is different' rests on AI systems gathering high-resolution behavioural data (latency, hesitancy, error patterns) and adapting to it in real time, grounded in encoding, retrieval and working-memory research rather than being digitised worksheets like past ed-tech.

Tom Perry's review of cognitive science in real classrooms found retrieval-practice effects are consistently positive and replicable in lab studies but much smaller and more variable in actual school implementation -- the evidence base behind Hendrick calling classroom retrieval practice 'the most lethally mutated thing in education.'

Alpha School's model complicates easy dismissal: chatbots and phones are banned, the AI does the sequencing and monitoring, and 'guides' give one-to-one attention driven by system data -- though at $40,000+ a year with no public outcome data, scrutiny is still warranted.

Curriculum sequencing is one of the hardest skills in teaching and most teachers never fully develop it through trial and error alone; Hendrick believes AI can capture the 'semantic gravity' judgment of expert curriculum designers and make it available at scale.

Because most cognitive-science findings come from small lab studies (around 40 postgraduates), Hendrick predicts that data from millions of AI-tutored student interactions could resolve long-standing open questions -- like optimal spacing schedules -- within two to five years.
quotes: if learning is a biological process governed by the laws of biology and physics, then it is measurable. And if it is measurable, it is designable.

Carl described a common pattern: students learn six words on a Monday, cram on Sunday night, score five or six out of six on Monday’s quiz, and then never encounter those words again in any structured way.

chatbots are banned. Mobile phones are banned. This is not kids messing about on ChatGPT. The AI is doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes – sequencing knowledge, monitoring attention, gathering data.
the paradox is that students at Alpha may get more individual tutor time than students in a traditional classroom of 30.
most of what we know comes from studies of 40 postgraduate students in a lab. The signal-to-noise ratio, as Carl put it, is low.
Carl’s prediction is bold: in the next two to five years, we are going to discover things about learning that we have been trying to figure out for decades.
